city.name: Carthage
summary: Founded, by tradition, by Phoenician settlers from Tyre in 814 BC, Carthage became the capital of a trading empire and one of the largest cities of the Mediterranean.

Scrub the timeline to see the Punic city with its famous circular naval harbour, Scipio's siege works of 147 BC, the ruins left in 146 BC, and the Roman grid city that rose on top a century later. Slide 'Then ⟷ Today' to compare with the town today: the harbours still show from the air.
city.note: Coastline and harbours traced from satellite imagery; monument positions from Wikipedia and excavation plans. District street blocks are schematic, and the line of the land walls is uncertain.

properties.name: Gulf of Tunis
properties.description: Carthage faced the open sea. Its fleets and merchant ships made it the richest city of the western Mediterranean.

properties.name: Lake of Tunis
properties.description: A shallow lagoon south-west of the city, separated from the sea by a sandbar, the taenia.

properties.name: Byrsa hill
description: The citadel hill. Legend says Queen Dido was offered as much land as an ox-hide could cover, cut the hide into thin strips and encircled the whole hill. 'Byrsa' is Greek for hide.
Today the Carthage National Museum and the old cathedral of Saint Louis stand on top.

images.caption: Model of the houses on the Byrsa slope, National Museum of Carthage
Model of the Byrsa quarter, another view

properties.name: Megara
properties.description: The garden suburb north of the city, inside the walls: villas, orchards, vegetable plots and cemeteries. Roman soldiers broke into it first in 147 BC.

properties.name: Punic city
description: Streets of flat-roofed houses, workshops and shrines on a regular grid running down to the sea. Wealthy houses had courtyards, cisterns and mosaic floors.
Appian describes six-storey buildings lining the three streets up to the citadel, fought for house by house in the final assault of 146 BC.

images.caption: Model of the Magon quarter by the sea, National Museum of Carthage

properties.name: Byrsa citadel
properties.description: The walled summit of the Byrsa, the last refuge of the defenders in 146 BC.

properties.name: Temple of Eshmun
properties.description: Carthage's greatest temple, to the god of healing, on top of the Byrsa, reached by sixty steps. In 146 BC its last defenders, including Roman deserters, set it on fire and died in it rather than surrender.

properties.name: Magon quarter
properties.description: A seafront district excavated by German archaeologists, with houses and the city's sea wall and gate. Named after a Carthaginian family.

images.file: Quartier Magon Carthage maquette porte mer.JPG
images.caption: Model of the sea gate in the Magon quarter

properties.name: 'Hannibal quarter'
properties.description: A planned district of houses with courtyards and cisterns built on the south slope of the Byrsa around 200 BC, in Hannibal's time.

properties.name: Agora
properties.description: The main square near the harbours, where the council of elders and the people's assembly met.

properties.name: Streets to the Byrsa
properties.description: Appian's three streets climbing from the agora to the citadel, where the Romans fought their way up in 146 BC.

properties.name: Circular naval harbour
description: The secret of Carthage's sea power: a circular basin ringed by ship sheds for 220 warships (Appian), with columns in front of each shed, so that it looked like a colonnade from the water.
It was hidden behind walls and reached only through the merchant harbour, so no one could see what was being built inside.

images.caption: Model of the naval harbour, National Museum of Carthage

properties.name: Ship sheds
properties.description: Slipways where warships were hauled out of the water, roofed and stored.

properties.name: Admiral's island
properties.description: A round island in the middle of the naval harbour, with more ship sheds and the admiral's headquarters, from which he could see out to sea and signal the fleet.

properties.name: Merchant harbour
properties.description: The harbour for merchant ships, opening to the sea to the south. Originally rectangular; its outline survives as the lagoon you can see today.

properties.name: Harbour entrance
properties.description: The single entrance from the sea, about 20 metres wide, closed with iron chains.

properties.name: Tophet
description: A sacred precinct of the gods Baal Hammon and Tanit, with thousands of urns of the cremated remains of infants and young animals beneath carved stone markers, spanning six centuries.

Greek, Roman and biblical writers said Carthaginians sacrificed children. Some scholars argue it was a cemetery for children who died young; most now think at least some were sacrifices, but the debate continues.

properties.name: Sea wall
properties.description: A single wall along the shore. The Romans finally broke in from the harbour side in spring 146 BC.

properties.name: Triple land wall
properties.description: Across the isthmus Carthage was defended by a triple line of walls, the main one about 13 metres high, with stables for 300 elephants and 4,000 horses built into it, according to Appian. Its exact line is still uncertain.

properties.name: Scipio's siege lines
properties.description: In 147 BC Scipio Aemilianus cut the city off by land with a fortified trench and wall right across the isthmus.

properties.name: Scipio's mole
properties.description: Scipio built a great stone mole across the harbour mouth to starve the city. The Carthaginians answered by secretly digging a new channel to the sea and launching a fleet built in the harbour.

properties.name: Ruins of Carthage
description: After the city fell it burned for days. Survivors were sold into slavery, the walls were levelled and the site was cursed and left empty for a century.
The story that the Romans sowed it with salt is a modern invention.

properties.name: Roman Carthage
description: Refounded as a Roman colony in 29 BC on a new grid that ignored the Punic streets: blocks of 120 by 480 Roman feet (about 35 by 141 metres). It grew into the second city of the western empire, rich on African grain and olive oil.
Augustine studied here, and in AD 439 it fell to the Vandals.

properties.name: Forum on the Byrsa
properties.description: The Romans sliced off the top of the Byrsa and buried the Punic houses beneath a vast platform for their forum, basilica and capitol. That is why the Hannibal quarter survived to be excavated.

properties.name: Cardo maximus
properties.description: The main north–south street of the Roman grid, through the forum.

properties.name: Decumanus maximus
properties.description: The main east–west street, from the forum down to the sea.

properties.name: Antonine Baths
properties.description: Among the largest baths in the Roman world, built AD 145–162 right on the seafront, with furnaces and service corridors in the basement and vaulted halls above.

properties.name: Amphitheatre
properties.description: Where the Christian martyrs Perpetua and Felicity were killed by wild beasts in AD 203.

properties.name: Circus
properties.description: A chariot-racing track about 570 metres long, one of the biggest outside Rome.

properties.name: Theatre
properties.description: The Roman theatre, where Augustine later confessed to loving the shows as a student.

properties.name: Odeon
properties.description: A roofed concert hall built around AD 207 for the Pythian games.

properties.name: La Malga cisterns
properties.description: Huge reservoirs at the end of the aqueduct, holding water for the city.

properties.name: Zaghouan aqueduct
properties.description: Built under Hadrian to carry water 132 km from the springs of Zaghouan.
